interactions.summary: Jiang says Dante's true mission is to reach heaven and write the Divine Comedy, and marvels at the poem's total design by comparing it to conceiving an entire television series before episode one is written.

The room asks whether Dante wrote Inferno first and how such coherence is possible; Jiang answers that he published Inferno first but could sustain the whole structure because Inferno, Purgatory, and Paradiso were real worlds and real people to him.
A participant reads the passage in which Beatrice explains why hell cannot harm her and introduces the heavenly chain involving the gentle lady and Lucia.

claims.claim: Jiang argues that teaching Paradiso first makes the construction of the whole poem legible because the class can then see how the beginning locks into the ending.
Jiang states that Dante published Inferno first and later published Purgatory and Paradiso, yet the poem contains no inconsistencies across those realms.
Jiang explains the poem's coherence by saying Inferno, Purgatory, and Paradiso were more real to Dante than ordinary life, so he encountered real persons there rather than mere figments.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compares Dante's feat to already having all ten seasons of a television series in mind before writing episode one.
signature_moments.source_phrase: write the entire TV series, all 10 seasons, even before you begin to write episodes
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives a vivid contemporary analogy for the poem's architectural completeness.

signature_moments.moment: For Dante, the three realms were real worlds populated by real people with their own psychology.
signature_moments.source_phrase: they're more real to him than his own world
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's strongest explanatory model for why the Comedy feels internally total and coherent.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Treated as a fully designed totality whose beginning and ending were conceived as one coherent structure.
The three realms are discussed as mutually coherent worlds that Dante experiences as real rather than invented scenery.
Named in the quoted heavenly chain as the figure called to assist Dante's rescue.

chronology_notes.note: This packet is where Jiang explicitly defends his reverse teaching order and links Dante's publication order to a theory of imaginative world-reality.

uncertainty_notes.note: The quoted reading contains ASR corruption in the middle of Beatrice's speech, but the core point about fearlessness and heavenly authorization remains clear.
